DEPARTMENT 307 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 25STCV01197    Hearing Date: July 6, 2026    Dept: 307

 

# 14 TENTATIVE RULING 9:15 a.m., Tuesday, July 7, 2027 

 

RUBEN HERNANDEZ v. LOS ANGELES COUNTY METROPOLITAN TRANSPORTATION AUTHORITY [25STCV01197] 

 

MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT OF DEFENDANT LOS ANGELES COUNTY METROPOLITAN TRANSPORTATION AUTHORITY 

 

NOTICE: OK [Pursuant to oral stipulation on 4/2/2026, the Court waived the MSJ notice period and advanced the 6/17/2026 hearing to 4/30/2026 to avoid a trial continuance. The MSJ hearing was later continued to 7/7/2026.] 

 

TIMELINE: Premises liability action on public property 

 

5/7/2024: Plaintiff Ruben Hernandez (“Plaintiff”), an employee of the security company Allied Universal, was assigned to provide security services at a train station operated by Defendant Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (“Metro”). (Perez Decl., Exh. D, at pp. 36:15-38:14.) Around 10:00pm, Plaintiff clocked out of work and was traveling home on a Metro-operated train through the Westlake/MacArthur Park Metro Station. On the train, Plaintiff was physically assaulted by another passenger, Cross-Defendant Lorenzo Byrd (“Byrd”). (Metro Exh. 4 [SAC], at p. 4.) Plaintiff alleges Metro failed to protect him because the train had insufficient non-policing safety measures in place at the time of the assault. (Id.; Metro Exh. 1.) 

 

1/16/2025: Hernandez files the Complaint. (Metro Exh. 2.) The operative Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”), filed 8/29/2025, alleges causes of action for: 

 

  1. Negligence (Common Carrier) 

  1. Premises Liability (Gov. Code, § 835) 

 

2/3/2025: Plaintiff files a workers’ compensation claim with Allied Universal (Case No. ADJ20467043). (Metro Exh. 3.) 

 

9/5/2025: Metro files its Answer to the SAC. (Metro Exh. 5.) 

 

12/9/2025: Metro files a Cross-Complaint against Byrd for indemnity, equitable contribution, apportionment, and declaratory relief. (Metro Exh. 6.) 

 

3/23/2026: Metro files this Motion for Summary Judgment as to the SAC, followed by Plaintiff’s Opposition (4/9/2026) and Metro’s Reply (4/17/2026). 

 

4/28/2026: Pursuant to Plaintiff’s Ex Parte Application, the Court continues the MSJ hearing to 7/7/2026 and orders the deposition of Metro’s PMK to be completed on or before 5/8/2026. 

 

5/11/2026: Metro’s PMK is deposed. 

 

6/10/2026: The Court continues Plaintiff’s Ex Parte Application for an Order Shortening Time to Hear Plaintiff’s Motion to Compel Further Deposition of Metro’s PMK to be heard concurrently with the MSJ on 7/7/2026. 

 

6/17/2026: Plaintiff files a Supplemental Opposition to the MSJ, which is followed by Metro’s Supplemental Reply (6/26/2026). 

 

TENTATIVE RULING: MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT OF DEFENDANT LOS ANGELES COUNTY METROPOLITAN TRANSPORTATION AUTHORITY is DENIED for failure to provide discovery as ordered. 

 

I.  MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT 

 

Metro moves for summary judgment on the SAC in its favor on the grounds that the incident between Plaintiff and Byrd was neither foreseeable nor preventable by Metro and its employees. (Mot., at p. 2.) 

 

There is no dispute that Metro, as a common carrier owed¿Plaintiff a duty of care. (Civ. Code, § 2100¿[“A carrier of persons for reward must use the utmost care and diligence for their safe carriage, must provide everything necessary for that purpose, and must exercise to that end a reasonable degree of skill.”].) “Common carriers bind themselves to carry safely those whom they take into their¿vehicles, and¿owe both a duty of utmost care and the vigilance of¿a very cautious¿person towards their passengers. Such carriers¿are responsible for¿any, even the slightest, negligence and are required to do all that human care, vigilance, and foresight¿reasonably can¿do under all the circumstances.” (Acosta v. Southern Cal. Rapid Transit Dist.¿(1970) 2 Cal.3d 19, 26.)  

 

“[T]he duty imposed upon carriers by Civil Code section 2100 includes a duty to protect passengers from assaults by fellow passengers.” (Lopez v. Southern Cal. Rapid Transit Dist. (1985) 40 Cal.3d 780, 785 (Lopez).) “This duty can only arise if in the exercise of the required degree of care the carrier has or should have knowledge of conditions from which it may reasonably be apprehended that an assault on a passenger may occur … and has the ability in the exercise of that degree of care to prevent the injury.” (Id. at p. 786.) “The fact that certain ‘precautionary measures’ would have the effect of protecting passengers from criminal assaults does not transform them into ‘police protection services.’” (Id. at p. 792.) 

 

Here, Metro argues that the attack on Plaintiff was neither foreseeable nor preventable because, as Plaintiff alleges, Byrd punched Plaintiff just one time and immediately exited the train, leaving inadequate time for the train operator to intervene. (Mot., at p. 6.) Metro also argues that at the time of the incident Plaintiff was still wearing his security guard uniform and was equipped with defensive weapons and handcuffs, so Metro’s employee would have been justified in believing that Plaintiff was the security officer handling the incident. (Id. at pp. 6-7.) 

 

Plaintiff responds that the foreseeability and preventability of the assault are questions of fact because sufficient evidence exists, or is likely to exist, to demonstrate that the Metro train operator (or other Metro employees) knew or should have known that unsafe conditions were developing on the train prior to Plaintiff’s assault such that the incident could have been predicted and mitigated. (Lopez, supra, 40 Cal.3d at p. 786.) For example, Byrd was loudly and aggressively harassing an elderly woman and panhandling on the Metro train even before he attacked Plaintiff. (Supp. Opp., at p. 3.) Plaintiff further argues that the Metro train line had a documented violence problem in the months preceding the attack and that Metro had multiple operational personnel assigned and stationed who failed to meet Metro’s published safety standards. (Id. at pp. 3-4.) Plaintiff further contends that Defendants have still failed to adequately respond to discovery intended to clarify whether Metro designed or maintained its trains without any operational ability to observe developing violence in the train’s passenger compartments. (Id. at p. 4.) Plaintiff continues to seek further discovery to determine the following relevant facts: (1) who was watching the Rail Operations Center (ROC) monitors when Byrd was harassing the woman before attacking Plaintiff; (2) whether CCTV at any of the stations along the Metro train line before the attack captured either when Byrd boarded or how long his aggressive behavior had been going on; (3) what the assigned (on-duty) security personnel were doing at the time of the attack; (4) whether the train operator had any means of observing what was happening in the cars behind them; and (5) why CCTV footage from this incident no longer exists in Metro’s records. (Ibid.) These facts are essential to determining whether the foreseeability and preventability of Plaintiff’s assault should be determined by the jury and are therefore integral to Plaintiff’s defense against this motion. 

 

The Court has already continued this MSJ hearing pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 437c, subdivision (h) to permit Plaintiff to conduct additional discovery on these factual questions and simultaneously ordered the deposition of Metro’s PMK to be conducted by 5/8/2026. (Minute Order, 4/28/2026.) Although an initial deposition occurred on 5/11/2026, Plaintiff contends that Metro’s PMK admitted that he had not prepared for the deposition and, thus, could not meaningfully answer Plaintiff’s questions. (Ortiz Depo. Tr., at pp. 9:5-10:3, 10:5-10, 97:8-10, 121:2-7, 204:6-23; Perez Decl., ¶¶ 4, 6-8, 14-15, Exhs. B, D, G.) Plaintiff’s expert witness has also submitted a declaration confirming that Metro’s PMK deposition failed to provide the foundational factual testimony necessary for his intended analysis of transit-safety, particularly concerning prior incidents of violence and line- and station-specific crime trends, CCTV configuration/retention/preservation, dispatch/CAD/ROC materials, security staffing and actual deployment, Allied Universal reporting protocols, and hazard management. (Pl.’s Exh. G, ¶¶ 4-5.) In light of Plaintiff’s position that the 5/11/2026 PMK deposition was not reasonably responsive to the deposition request, Plaintiff has since filed an Ex Parte Application for an order shortening time to hear Plaintiff’s Motion to Compel Further Deposition of Metro’s PMK, which is scheduled to be heard on the same date as this MSJ hearing. (Minute Order, 7/10/2026.) Accordingly, Plaintiff is now requesting relief under Code of Civil Procedure section 437, subdivision (i) for Metro’s unreasonable failure to cooperate with the court-ordered deposition. 

 

“If, after granting a continuance to allow specified additional discovery, the court determines that the party seeking summary judgment has unreasonably failed to allow the discovery to be conducted, the court shall grant a continuance to permit the discovery to go forward or deny the motion for summary judgment or summary adjudication. This section does not affect or limit the ability of a party to compel discovery…”¿ (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (i), italics added.) The same policies underlying Code of Civil Procedure section 437c, subdivision (h) pertain to subdivision (i). Specifically, “summary judgment is a drastic measure which deprives the losing party of trial on the merits.” (Dee v. Vintage Petroleum, Inc.¿(2003) 106 Cal.App.4th 30,¿34-35.) “To mitigate summary judgment's harshness,” the Legislature intended the relief available under subdivisions (h) and (i) to be virtually mandatory, rather than discretionary. (Ibid.) “Where the opposing party¿submits¿an adequate affidavit showing that essential facts may exist but cannot be presented¿timely, the court¿must¿either deny summary judgment or grant a continuance.” (Ibid.) 

 

Here, as described above, Metro’s MSJ raises a narrow issue: that no triable factual issues exist with respect to the foreseeability and preventability of the attack on Plaintiff. Metro’s argument is premised on two primary inferences: (1) that Metro’s train operator was unable to intervene because the attack was brief, and (2) even if the train operator could have intervened, the operator was reasonable in believing that Plaintiff himself was already responding to the scene as a security officer. These factual conclusions place Plaintiff’s factual discovery squarely at issue, including but not limited to the extent to which the train operator and other Metro personnel had the ability to monitor the train’s passenger compartment and/or communicate about potential security threats, the extent to which Byrd’s movements were observable on the live CCTV footage prior to the incident, the extent to which Metro personnel could and did engage in internal dispatch/CAD/ROC/SOC communications, Metro’s staffing records, and the extent of Allied Universal’s duties. (Supp. Opp., at p. 5.) Such facts are directly relevant to the questions of whether the train operator did or should have had notice of Byrd’s escalating conduct prior to the incident and whether Metro’s employees had the mechanisms in place to meaningfully intervene in light of such notice. (Id. at p. 7.) 

 

Under Lopez, if Metro had notice of Byrds’ potential aggressive conduct, the question of whether the train operator “should not have taken some steps to maintain or restore order before tempers got so far out of control that he was powerless to prevent the injury which occurred to plaintiff” is a factual question for the jury. (Lopez, supra, 40 Cal.3d at p. 786.) As a result, Plaintiff would be prejudiced by considering the merits of this MSJ prior to ensuring that he has had an adequate and meaningful opportunity to discover the facts pertaining to notice, including the extent to which passenger violence were known hazards on the specific Metro train line, what Metro knew or could have known before and during the incident between Byrd and Plaintiff, and what systems and personnel were in place and/or functional to detect and respond to escalating altercations. (Supp. Opp., at p. 7.) Accordingly, the Court agrees that the facts identified by Plaintiff are essential to his opposition to this MSJ. 

 

The Court also finds that Metro has unreasonably failed to enable Plaintiff’s discovery to be conducted. Metro’s MSJ was originally set to be heard on 4/30/2026. The Court continued the hearing and ordered Metro to produce a PMK witness by 5/8/2026. As referenced above, when the deposition finally occurred on 5/11/2026, Metro’s PMK admitted that he was not prepared: he had not yet reviewed any documents, had not performed any investigation into the noticed topics for the deposition, had not spoken to any individuals other than Metro’s counsel, and had not even learned of Plaintiff’s assault until just one week prior to the deposition. (Ortiz Depo. Tr., 9:5-10:3, 204:6-23.) This testimony confirms that Metro did not produce an adequately prepared witness to comply with the court-ordered deposition. (Supp. Opp., at pp. 8-9.) Plaintiff’s pending Ex Parte Application also details examples of the delays and lack of cooperation exhibited by Metro’s counsel in both procuring a knowledgeable deposition witness and in conducting the deposition itself, even after the Court already granted a continuance to permit the very deposition that is the subject of this Code of Civil Procedure section 437, subdivision (i) request. Under the circumstances, Metro’s argument that it “allowed” the discovery by producing the requisite witness at the May 11 deposition is unpersuasive. (See Rep. p. 8.) Metro’s production of a PMK witness who was ill-prepared to meaningfully respond to Plaintiff’s questions constituted a significant interference with Plaintiff’s intended discovery and created an undue delay in hearing this MSJ. 

 

Finally, although the Court has already continued the trial from 5/11/2026 to 8/3/2026 to accommodate the need to conduct further discovery, the Court has repeatedly admonished the parties to avoid any further trial continuance. Plaintiff’s opposition is quite clear that he is not seeking to continue the jury trial in this matter, which is less than 30 days away from this MSJ hearing. (The Final Status Conference is scheduled for 7/24/2026.) At this juncture, a further continuance to permit this motion to be heard on the merits would simply delay trial and reward Metro for its uncooperative tactics. Considering the totality of the circumstances, the Court finds that Metro’s unreasonably delay in complying with the Court’s order compelling the PMK deposition warrants the denial of summary judgment. 

 

Therefore, Metro’s motion for summary judgment is DENIED pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 437c, subdivision (i). 

 

II. EVIDENTIARY OBJECTIONS 

 

Metro objects to the Declaration of Hector C. Perez, including Exhs. H and I (Nos. 1-3, 6) and the Supplemental Declaration of Dr. Berkowitz (Nos. 4-5). The Court declines to rule on the following objections at this time: 1, 2, and 3. The following evidentiary objections are OVERRULED: 4, 5, and 6. 

 

III.  REQUESTS FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE 

 

Metro requests judicial notice of the following documents: 

 

  1. Plaintiff’s Claim for Damages (dated 7/16/2024) (Metro Exh. 1); 

  1. Plaintiff’s Complaint (filed 1/16/2025) (Metro Exh. 2); 

  1. Case Information Sheet from Division of Workers’ Compensation (Case No. ADJ20467043) (Metro Exh. 3); 

  1. Plaintiff’s SAC (filed 8/29/2025) (Metro Exh. 4); 

  1. Metro’s Answer to the SAC (filed 9/5/2025) (Metro Exh. 5); 

  1. Metro’s Cross-Complaint (filed 12/9/2025) (Metro Exh. 6). 

 

The Court takes judicial notice of the existence of Plaintiff’s Claim for Damages filed with Metro pursuant to Evidence Code section 452, subdivision (c), but not the truth of the facts asserted therein. 

 

The Court takes judicial notice of the existence of the above-identified pleadings in this matter and the existence of Plaintiff’s Worker’s Compensation case pursuant to Evidence Code section 452, subdivision (d), but not the truth of the facts asserted therein. 

 

Defendant Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority to serve notice of ruling.

This tentative ruling (“TR”) shall be the order of the Court unless changed at the hearing and shall by this reference be incorporated into the Minute Order. TR emailed to counsel and posted to court’s website on 7/6/26 at 2 p.m. 

Case Number: 25STCV19071    Hearing Date: July 6, 2026    Dept: 307

 

# 13 TENTATIVE RULING 9:15 a.m., Tuesday, July 7, 2026 

 

DANIELLE UWAOMA v. WILSHIRE CREST HOTEL, et al. [25STCV19071] 

 

DEMURRER TO THE COMPLAINT OF DEFENDANT THE WILSHIRE CREST HOTEL, LLC 

 

MEET AND CONFER: DEFECTIVE The Hotel’s counsel attempted to meet and confer by telephone, left two voicemail messages for Plaintiff’s counsel, and sent two emails to Plaintiff’s counsel, but it does not appear that Plaintiff’s counsel responded to the meet and confer attempts. (Fischer Decl., ¶ 5.) 

 

BACKGROUND: Complaint alleges battery, negligence, premises liability, IIED, fraud, etc. arising from bedbug bites during hotel stay 

 

TIMELINE: 

 

7/28/2023: Plaintiff Danielle Uwaoma (“Plaintiff”) checks into Defendant Wilshire Crest Hotel (the “Hotel”) and is assigned to a guest room. Plaintiff alleges that Defendants Joseph Tomaszewski (“J. Tomaszewski”) and Guerta Tomaszewski (“G. Tomaszewski”) own, operate, and manage the Hotel.  

 

7/29/2023: Plaintiff discovers that she has bed bug bites across her body. Plaintiff immediately reports the bites to the Hotel’s front desk staff, and the staff reassigns Plaintiff to a new guest room. 

 

7/30/2023: Plaintiff checks out of the Hotel. 

 

8/4/2023: When Plaintiff seeks medical treatment, she is diagnosed with bed bug bites and is prescribed medication. Plaintiff alleges that she still has physical scars and emotional distress from the bites. 

 

6/30/2025: Plaintiff files the Complaint, alleging causes of action for:  
 

  1. Battery 

  1. Negligence 

  1. Premises Liability 

  1. Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress (“IIED”) 

  1. Fraudulent Concealment 

  1. Private Nuisance 

  1. Public Nuisance 

  1. Breach of Contract 

 

6/5/2026: The Hotel files this Demurrer. As of 7/2/2026, Plaintiff has not filed an Opposition. 

 

TENTATIVE RULING: DEMURRER TO THE COMPLAINT OF DEFENDANT THE WILSHIRE CREST HOTEL, LLC is OVERRULED in part, SUSTAINED with LEAVE TO AMEND in part, and SUSTAINED without leave to amend in part. 

 

I. DEMURRER 

 

The Hotel demurs to the first, fourth, fifth, and sixth causes of action in Plaintiff’s Complaint pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 430.10, subdivisions (e) and (f) on the grounds that Plaintiff fails to state a claim against the Hotel and that the claims are so uncertain as to preclude the Hotel from meaningfully responding to said claims.1 

 

  1. 1st Cause of Action: Battery — OVERRULED 

 

Plaintiff’s battery claim is adequately pled. “The essential elements of a cause of action for battery are: (1) defendant touched plaintiff, or caused plaintiff to be touched, with the intent to harm or offend plaintiff; (2) plaintiff did not consent to the touching; (3) plaintiff was harmed or offended by defendant’s conduct; and (4) a¿reasonable person in plaintiff’s position would have been offended by¿the touching.”¿(Yun¿Hee¿So v.¿Sook¿Ja Shin¿(2013) 212 Cal.App.4th 652, 669; see CACI, No. 1300.)¿“[T]he element of intent is satisfied if the evidence shows defendant acted with a “willful disregard” of the plaintiff's rights.” (Ashcraft v. King (1991) 228 Cal.App.3d 604, 613.) 

 

Here, Plaintiff alleges that the bed bug bites constituted a harmful or offensive contact with her body and that the Hotel acted with intent by recklessly failing to warn Plaintiff of the dangerous bed bug infestation despite its prior knowledge of the infestation. (Compl.,¿¶¶ 49-50.) The Hotel argues that Plaintiff fails demonstrate the intent element of her claim because Plaintiff has not alleged that an authorized representative of the Hotel acted with the requisite intent to harm or offend. “Typically, a corporation may be liable for employee misconduct under a respondeat superior theory.” (C.R. v. Tenet Healthcare Corp. (2009) 169 Cal.App.4th 1094, 1110.) “As an alternate theory to respondeat superior, an employer may be liable for an employee's act where the employer either authorized the tortious act or subsequently ratified an originally unauthorized tort.” (Ibid.)  

 

In this case, Plaintiff expressly alleges that Defendants, including the Hotel’s owners and managers J. Tomaszewski and G. Tomaszewski, in the management of their hotel’s housekeeping and maintenance both authorized and ratified the Hotel staff’s failure to ensure sanitary conditions in the Hotel, including the failure to regularly change bed sheets and bed skirts, to inspect bed mattresses and headboards, and to specifically inspect for bed bugs. (Compl., ¶¶ 33, 35-36.) Plaintiff further alleges that the Hotel’s managers failed to take action to investigate and discipline housekeeping and maintenance staff when informed of prior bed bug infestation incidents. (Id. ¶ 34.) Plaintiff also alleges that the Hotel, through its managers, knew of the bed bug infestation and nevertheless failed to take the necessary steps to eliminate the infestation, thereby causing Plaintiff to be bitten. (Id. ¶¶ 54-56.) These allegations are sufficient, for pleading purposes, to demonstrate that the Hotel’s managers (who are specifically named as defendants) knowingly authorized and ratified the tortious conduct of their housekeeping and maintenance employees. Such allegations support a showing that the Hotel’s managers acted in reckless and willful disregard of the offensive and harmful contact to Plaintiff. (Id. ¶¶ 37-39, 49, 52-54.) Accordingly, the Hotel has not shown that Plaintiff fails to adequately pled the intent element of her battery claim. 

 

Therefore, the Hotel’s demurrer to the first cause of action for battery is OVERRULED. 

 

  1. 4th Cause of Action: IIED — SUSTAINED with LEAVE TO AMEND 

 

Plaintiff’s IIED claim is inadequately pled. To establish¿a cause of action for IIED, a¿plaintiff must show:¿“(1) outrageous conduct by the defendant; (2) the defendant's intention of causing or reckless disregard of the probability of causing emotional distress; (3) the plaintiff's suffering severe or extreme emotional distress; and (4) actual and proximate causation of the emotional distress by the defendant's outrageous conduct.” (Trerice¿v. Blue Cross of California¿(1989) 209 Cal.App.3d 878, 883.) To be “outrageous,” conduct must be so extreme as to exceed all bounds of decency in a civilized community. (Potter v. Firestone Tire & Rubber Co. (1993) 6 Cal.4th 965, 1001.) 

 

Here, Plaintiff alleges that Defendants collectively chose not to eradicate the Hotel’s bed bug infestation, which caused Plaintiff emotional harm, in willful disregard of their knowledge of prior infestations in the Hotel and in Plaintiff’s guest room. (Compl., ¶¶ 86-87.) Once again, the Hotel argues that Plaintiff has not alleged facts which establish that the Hotel’s authorized representatives acted with the requisite intent to cause Plaintiff emotional harm. For the same reasons discussed above with respect to Plaintiff’s battery claim, however, the Court disagrees. 

 

Next, the Hotel also argues that Plaintiff fails to adequately plead that she suffered the level of severe or extreme emotional distress as a result of the bed bug infestation that is necessary to support a claim for IIED. On this point, the Court agrees. IIED results when a defendant's conduct “has a severe and traumatic effect on the plaintiff's emotional tranquility.” (Kraslawsky¿v. Upper Deck Co.¿(1997) 56 Cal.4th 179, 194.)¿“Only emotional distress of ‘such substantial quantity or enduring quality’ that an individual in civilized society should not be expected to endure it constitutes severe emotional distress.” (Angie M. v. Superior Court¿(1995) 37 Cal.App.4th 1217, 1227.)  

 

Here, Plaintiff merely alleges that she has suffered “present and ongoing emotional distress.” (Compl., ¶ 86.) Plaintiff also alleges that she incurred medical expenses as a result of the Hotel’s conduct. (Id. ¶ 94.) These limited, vague facts fail to demonstrate the heightened level of “severe and traumatic” effects on Plaintiff. Merely alleging that a plaintiff is suffering¿from distress (even where the distress leads to physical or medical symptoms) without identifying how¿the emotional distress was severe and pervasive in quality and quantity is insufficient to survive the demurrer stage. (Kiseskey¿v. Carpenters' Trust for So. California¿(1983) 144 Cal.App.3d 222, 232 [“testimony of plaintiffs that they were “upset” and “disturbed” and “furious” did not meet the requisite test” for severe emotional distress]; see Wong v. Tai Jing¿(2010) 189 Cal.App.4th 1354, 1376 [evidence of losing sleep, upset stomach and anxiety did not constitute severe emotional distress of such lasting and enduring quality that no reasonable person should be expected to endure].) Accordingly, the Court finds that Plaintiff fails to state a claim for IIED. 

 

Therefore, the Hotel’s demurrer to the fourth cause of action for IIED is SUSTAINED with LEAVE TO AMEND.¿  

 

  1. 5th Cause of Action: Fraudulent Concealment — OVERRULED 

 

Plaintiff’s fraudulent concealment claim is sufficiently pled. “[T]he elements of an action for fraud and deceit based on concealment are: (1) the defendant must have concealed or suppressed a material fact, (2) the defendant must have been under a duty to disclose the fact to the plaintiff, (3) the defendant must have intentionally concealed or suppressed the fact with the intent to defraud the plaintiff, (4) the plaintiff must have been unaware of the fact and would not have acted as he did if he had known of the concealed or suppressed fact, and (5) as a result of the concealment or suppression of the fact, the plaintiff must have sustained damage.” (Blickman¿Turkus, LP v. MF Downtown Sunnyvale, LLC¿(2008) 162 Cal.App.4th 858, 868, internal citation¿omitted.)¿“California courts apply the¿same specificity¿standard to¿evaluate the factual underpinnings of a fraudulent concealment claim at the pleading stage, even though the focus of inquiry shifts to the unique elements of the claim.”¿(Rattagan¿v. Uber Technologies, Inc.¿(2024) 17 Cal.5th 1, 43¿(Rattagan).)¿“The requirement of specificity in a fraud action against a corporation requires the plaintiff to allege the names of the persons who made the allegedly fraudulent representations, their authority to speak, to whom they spoke, what they said or wrote, and when it was said or written.” (Tarmann v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. (1991) 2 Cal.App.4th 153, 157.)¿¿ 

 

Here, Plaintiff alleges that the Hotel failed to warn her regarding the dangers of the bed bug infestation in her guest room. (Compl., ¶ 99.) More specifically, Plaintiff alleges that the Hotel’s “front desk personnel, hotel management, and housekeeping staff” were aware of the bed bug infestation and that the Hotel’s front desk personnel, who were authorized to speak on behalf of the Hotel, intentionally failed to disclose the bed bug infestation to Plaintiff during check-in. (Id. ¶¶ 29, 101-103.) These allegations adequately demonstrate who omitted the information from Plaintiff and their authority to speak on behalf of the Hotel (i.e. the front desk staff), what facts were not disclosed (i.e. the existence of an unresolved bed bug infestation), where and when the omission occurred (i.e. during the Hotel check-in process), and to whom they spoke (i.e. Plaintiff). Plaintiff also expressly alleges that the Hotel intended to deceive Plaintiff by taking advantage of Plaintiff’s lack of knowledge about the infestation in order to profit from her hotel stay. (Id. ¶ 108.) Although the Hotel argues that Plaintiff has not alleged facts establishing how the Hotel’s management was aware of the bed bug infestation, Plaintiff specifically alleges that the Hotel’s managers knew about the infestation based on their continuous monitoring of online guest reviews notifying the Hotel of bed bugs found at the Hotel. (Id. ¶¶ 26-27, 98, 100.) Taken together, the Court finds that these factual allegations are sufficiently specific to state a cause of action for fraud at the pleading stage. 

 

Therefore, the Hotel’s demurrer to the fifth cause of action for fraudulent concealment is OVERRULED. 

 

  1. 6th Cause of Action: Private Nuisance — SUSTAINED without leave to amend 

 

Plaintiff’s private nuisance claim is inadequately pled. To plead a claim for private¿nuisance, a plaintiff must¿allege¿that: (1)¿the defendant¿interfered¿with the plaintiff's use and enjoyment of the plaintiff's property, (2) the¿invasion of the plaintiff's interest in¿their¿use and enjoyment of¿the¿land was “substantial” (i.e. it caused plaintiff to suffer substantial actual damage), and (3) the interference with¿the plaintiff’s¿protected interest¿was “unreasonable”¿(i.e. it must be of such nature, duration, or amount as to constitute unreasonable interference with the plaintiff’s¿use and enjoyment of¿their¿land.)¿(San Diego Gas & Elec. Co. v. Superior Ct.¿(1996)¿13 Cal. 4th 893,¿938.) 

 

Here, the Hotel argues that Plaintiff cannot state a private nuisance claim because Plaintiff does not have an interest in the property at issue (i.e. her guest room in the Hotel). (Compl., ¶ 117.) “Although ‘any interest sufficient to be dignified as a property right’ will support an action based on a private nuisance, and this includes within its purview a tenancy for a term, such right does not inure in favor of a licensee, lodger or employee.” (Venuto v. Owens-Corning Fiberglas Corp. (1971) 22 Cal.App.3d 116, 125.) Here, Plaintiff’s allegation that she was a guest of the Hotel does not establish any interference with Plaintiff’s property right as a matter of law. Even if given the opportunity to plead additional facts, Plaintiff will be unable to cure this pleading defect. 

 

Therefore, the Hotel’s demurrer to the sixth cause of action for private nuisance is SUSTAINED without leave to amend. 

 

II. REQUESTS FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE 

 

The Hotel requests judicial notice of the following court documents in support of its demurrer: 

 

  1. Plaintiff’s Complaint in this action 

  1. Plaintiff’s Proof of Service as to the Hotel, filed 2/13/2026 

  1. The Hotel’s Articles of Organization, filed with the California Secretary of State in 2012 

  1. The Hotel’s 2023 and 2025 Statements of Information, filed with the California Secretary of State, reflecting that Aaron Tomaszewski was the Manager of the Limited Liability Company and the agent for service of process at all relevant times. 

 

The Hotel also requests judicial notice of the fact that no default or default judgment has been entered against the Hotel as of 6/8/2026. 

 

The Court takes judicial notice of Requests No. 1, 2, and 5 pursuant to Evidence Code section 452, subdivision (d) and of Requests No. 3 and 4 pursuant to Evidence Code section 452, subdivision (c). 

 

Defendant The Wilshire Crest Hotel, LLC to serve notice of ruling. This tentative ruling (“TR”) shall be the order of the Court unless changed at the hearing and shall by this reference be incorporated into the Minute Order. 

 

TR emailed to counsel and posted to court’s website on 7/6/26 at 2 p.m. 

 

Case Number: 26STCV01721    Hearing Date: July 6, 2026    Dept: 307

 

 

# 15   TENTATIVE RULING                9:15 a.m. Tuesday, July 7, 2027

 

DIPLOMAT PROPERTY MANAGER, LLC v. STEWART TITLE GUARANTY COMPANY, et al. [26STCV01721]

 

DEMURRER TO THE FIRST AMENDED COMPLAINT WITH A MOTION TO STRIKE OF DEFENDANT STEWART TITLE GUARANTY COMPANY

 

MEET AND CONFER: OK. Complies with CCP 430.41 and 435.5. 

 

BACKGROUND: FAC alleges breach of insurance contract and breach of the implied covenant (bad withholding of policy benefits)

 

TIMELINE:

 

Circa 2019 or 2020: Sound Equity, Inc. (“Lender”) considers making a loan in the amount of $2,279,700.00 (the “Loan”) to Palms Blvd. Venice Beach, LLC (“Borrower”) to be used to purchase the real property located at 722 and 724 Palms Blvd. Venice, CA 90291 (the “Property”) from Ginger Drinkwater (“Drinkwater”). The Loan was to be secured by a first priority lien position Deed of Trust recorded against the Property from Borrower to Lender. The Deed of Trust was to be recorded by Defendant Stewart Title of California, Inc. (“Stewart Escrow”) and insured by Defendant Stewart Title Guaranty Company (“Stewart Insurance”).

 

When Stewart Escrow’s escrow officer and notary public, Nancy Rico, asks Drinkwater to sign the Grant Deed for Borrower’s purchase, Drinkwater allegedly asks her son why she was being asked to sign the Grant Deed. Her son purportedly falsely tells Drinkwater that it needed to be signed to finalize the construction they were doing in the front of the house.

 

1/10/2020: Stewart Escrow closes escrow for the Loan, receives its fees as

escrow agent, disburses the Loan proceeds, records the Grant Deed from Drinkwater to Borrower, records the Deed of Trust in favor of Lender, and issues a Loan Policy of Title Insurance (the “Policy”) to Lender and its successors and/or assignees.

 

3/8/2021: Lender assigns the Deed of Trust to Sound Equity High Income Debt

Fund, LLC (“Debt Fund”). The assignment is recorded.

 

4/1/2021: Debt Fund files a Complaint for judicial foreclosure against Borrower

after Borrower defaults on the Loan.

 

3/24/2022: Drinkwater files a Complaint against Lender (the “Drinkwater

Action”) alleging that the Grant Deed was procured by fraud and without compensation, rendering the Deed of Trust invalid and unenforceable as a lien against the Property. Stewart Insurance had two in-house attorneys present at the trial in the Drinkwater Action and were therefore on notice of the Drinkwater Action. In total, ten lawsuits arising from the Loan and the Deed of Trust were ultimately filed (the “Covered Lawsuits”).

 

6/6/2022: After a foreclosure sale, Debt Fund assigns the Loan and the Deed of

Trust to Plaintiff Diplomat Property Manager, LLC (“Diplomat”). On the same date, a Trustee’s Deed Upon Sale is recorded, pursuant to which Diplomat becomes the owner of the Property.

 

12/22/2023: Lender tenders a claim against Stewart Insurance for its defense in

the Drinkwater Action.

 

1/18/2024: Stewart Insurance denies Lender’s tender on the grounds that

Diplomat, not Lender, was the party insured under the Policy and that the causes of action alleged in the Drinkwater Action were not covered by the Policy. (FAC, Exh. 13.)

 

1/16/2026: Diplomat files the Complaint. The operative First Amended

Complaint (“FAC”), filed 5/1/2026, alleges causes of action for:

1.   Breach of Contract By Agents and Fiduciaries for Failure to Strictly Comply with Escrow Instructions

2.   Breach of Insurance Contract

3.   Breach of the Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing

 

6/5/2026: Stewart Insurance files this Demurrer and Motion to Strike, which is

followed by Diplomat’s Opposition (6/23/2026) and Stewart Insurance’s Reply (6/29/2026).

 

TENTATIVE RULING: DEMURRER OF DEFENDANT STEWART TITLE GUARANTY COMPANY is SUSTAINED with LEAVE TO AMEND.

 

MOTION TO STRIKE OF DEFENDANT STEWART TITLE GUARANTY COMPANY is DENIED as MOOT.

 

I.        DEMURRER

 

Stewart Insurance demurs to the second and third causes of action in the FAC pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 430.10, subdivision (e) on the grounds that Diplomat fails to state facts sufficient to constitute the causes of action against Stewart Insurance.

 

A.           2nd Cause of Action: Breach of Insurance Contract – SUSTAINED with LEAVE TO AMEND

 

Diplomat fails to plead a claim for breach of insurance contract against Stewart Insurance. Insurance policies are a category of contract, and thus subject to the same general rules pertaining to any other contract. (Kransco v. American Empire Surplus Lines Ins. Co. (2000) 23 Cal.4th 390, 400.) “The burden is on the insured to establish that the claim is within the basic scope of coverage and on the insurer to establish that the claim is specifically excluded.” (MacKinnon v. Truck Ins. Exchange (2003) 31 Cal.4th 635, 648.) “When determining whether a particular policy provides a potential for coverage and a duty to defend, we are guided by the principle that interpretation of an insurance policy is a question of law.” (Waller v. Truck Ins. Exchange, Inc. (1995) 11 Cal.4th 1, 18.)¿

 

Here, the Policy names Lender and “its successors and/or assignees as their interests may appear” as the insured and was intended to insure that the Deed of Trust was recorded as a valid, enforceable first priority lien position Deed of Trust for the Property. (FAC, ¶¶ 21-22, Exhs. 3-5.) The “Covered Risk” under the Policy includes forgery and fraud, unmarketable title, and invalidity or unenforceability of the lien. (Id. Exh. 5.) Diplomat alleges that Stewart Insurance owed duties to Diplomat under the Policy, including the duty to defend, and breached said duties by, for example, failing to represent the insureds in the Covered Lawsuits. (Id. ¶ 56.) Specifically, Diplomat alleges that Stewart Insurance should have construed Lender’s tender of defense as being a tender on behalf of Diplomat and thus, Stewart Insurance should have provided Diplomat with reasonable assistance in pursuing a claim under the Policy. (Id. ¶ 36.) Diplomat further alleges that Stewart Insurance should have accepted the claim because of the infirmities in the Deed of Trust. (Id. ¶ 38.)

 

Stewart Insurance argues that it could not have breached the Policy by rejecting Lender’s tender because Lender was no longer covered by the Policy at the time of the defense tender. Specifically, Stewart Insurance asserts that the express and unambiguous terms of the Policy indicate that Lender’s insurance coverage terminated when it assigned its interest in the Deed of Trust to Debt Fund in March 2021 because Lender no longer held an interest in the Property. (FAC, ¶ 24; Exh. 6.) In its Denial Letter to Lender, Stewart Insurance stated that it had no duty to defend based on Condition 2 of the Policy, given the assignments and the foreclosure sale. (Id. ¶¶ 29-30, Exh. 10, 11, 13.) Condition 2 provides:

 

The coverage of this policy shall continue in force as of Date of Policy in favor of an Insured after acquisition of the Title by an Insured or after conveyance by an Insured, but only so long as the Insured retains an estate or interest in the Land, or holds an obligation secured by a purchase money Mortgage given by a purchaser from the Insured, or only so long as the Insured shall have liability by reason of warranties in any transfer or conveyance of the Title. […]

 

(Id. Exh. 5, at p. 7, italics added.) Stewart Insurance now argues that Lender had no right to coverage when the Drinkwater Action was filed in March 2022 or when it tendered its defense in December 2023 because Lender’s coverage under the Policy had already terminated under Condition 2 with the assignment of the Deed of Trust to Debt Fund in March 2021. (Mot., at p. 17.)

 

Diplomat responds that there was a breach of the Policy because warranties existed in each of the assignments which resulted in Lender and the assignees remaining insured under the Policy. (Opp., at pp. 7, 15.) Specifically, Diplomat contends that the assignment of a loan secured by a Deed of Trust contains the warranties governed by Commercial Code section 3416, which provides, “[a] person who transfers an instrument for consideration warrants all of the following to the transferee and, if the transfer is by indorsement, to any subsequent transferee … the warrantor is a person entitled to enforce the instrument …” (Comm. Code, § 3416, subd. (a)(1).) Commercial Code section 3416, however, governs transfer warranties for negotiable instruments, such as checks and promissory notes, and is not applicable to real property security instruments like the Deed of Trust here. Diplomat cites no authority for the position that either Commercial Code section 3416 (or the UCC generally) applies to a Deed of Trust securing an interest in real property. Instead, as Stewart Insurance argues, Civil Code section 1113 provides the applicable warranties referenced in the Policy here. (Fidelity National Title Ins. Co. v. Miller (1989) 215 Cal.App.3d 1163, 1171 [applying covenants of Civil Code section 1113 to title insurance dispute]; Pollard v. Saxe & Yolles Dev. Co. (1974) 12 Cal.3d 374, 380, fn. 5 [noting that Civil Code section 1113 “deals with warranties of title”].) As Lender never acquired “title” to the Property, Diplomat cannot show that the implied warranties under Civil Code section 1113 form a basis for continued coverage under the Policy.

 

Next, Diplomat argues that it never received a final or unconditional payment as a result of the Drinkwater Action, resulting in Diplomat remaining an insured under the Policy. (Opp., at pp. 7, 17.) Diplomat relies on Paramount Properties Co. v. Transamerica Title Ins. Co. (1970) 1 Cal.3d 562 (Paramount) which held, under the narrow facts in that case, that only final or unconditional payments in connection with claims would terminate the insured's risk connected with the validity of the title. (Id. at p. 569.) Even so, as Stewart Insurance extensively explains, the factual circumstances and legal issues addressed in Paramount are not analogous to the instant matter. Simply put, Paramount does not stand for the general proposition that insurance coverage continues indefinitely in all factual situations until a lender receives final and unconditional payment.

 

Third, Diplomat argues that Condition 2 of the Policy expressly provides that coverage will continue even if an insured acquires title at a foreclosure sale. (Opp., at p. 18.) Stewart Insurance responds, however, that Diplomat (not Lender) acquired title of the Property at the foreclosure sale. (FAC, ¶ 30, Exh. 11.) Because Diplomat became the owner of the Property by Trustee’s Deed, recorded on 6/6/2022 before Lender tendered its claim, Stewart Insurance argues that Lender had no interest in the Property and no rights under the Policy when it tendered its defense. (Rep., at p. 9.) Moreover, whether the Deed of Trust was void due to fraud is irrelevant to Lender’s legal interest in the Property at the time of the tender. Thus, neither of these arguments appear relevant to Diplomat’s claim that Stewart Insurance should have treated Lender’s tender of defense as a tender by Diplomat. Diplomat fails to allege that it was a defendant in the Drinkwater Action, and thus, Diplomat has not clarified how it was owed any duty to defend.

 

Fourth, Diplomat argues that Condition 2 is ambiguous because it gives no indication of the intent to terminate coverage while Lender’s primary risk survived. (Opp., at p. 18.) Yet, Diplomat fails to identify any specific language in Condition 2 that could be reasonably construed to mean that coverage would continue for Lender after it no longer retained any interest in the Property. Condition 2 plainly states that coverage would continue “only so long as the Insured retains an estate or interest in the Land.” (Id. Exh. 5, at p. 7, italics added.) This language unambiguously demonstrates the parties’ intent to limit the scope and duration of coverage for the Insureds. The fact that this section is entitled “Continuation of Coverage” instead of “Termination of Coverage” does not alter the plain meaning of the provision. As Diplomat does not show that Condition 2 is reasonably susceptible to multiple constructions, the Court must infer the intent of the parties from the four corners of the Policy alone.

 

Fifth, Diplomat argues that Section 2695.4(a) of the California Fair Claims Settlement Practices Regulations (the “Regulations”) required Stewart Insurance to construe the tender by Lender as being a tender on behalf of Diplomat. (Opp., at p. 20.) Section 2695.4(a) provides: “[e]very insurer shall disclose to a first party claimant or beneficiary, all benefits, coverage, time limits or other provisions of any insurance policy issued by that insurer that may apply to the claim presented by the claimant. When additional benefits might reasonably be payable under an insured's policy upon receipt of additional proofs of claim, the insurer shall immediately communicate this fact to the insured and cooperate with and assist the insured in determining the extent of the insurer's additional liability.” Diplomat concludes, without meaningful factual analysis, that Stewart Insurance concealed “what benefits might reasonably be payable” in violation of Section 2695.4. (Opp., at p. 20.) Even so, Diplomat fails to clearly explain why Section 2695.4 must be construed as requiring Stewart Insurance to interpret Lender’s tender for its defense in the Drinkwater Action as a tender on behalf of Diplomat for all ten of the Covered Lawsuits. (Rep., at p. 13.)

 

By contrast, Section 2695.5(e) of the Regulations makes clear that the insurer owes responsibilities to the “claimant” upon receiving a notice of claim. Section 2695.2(c) defines “claimant” as “a first or third party claimant as defined in these regulations…” Section 2695.2(f) defines “first party claimant” as “any person asserting a right under an insurance policy as a named insured, other insured or beneficiary under the terms of that insurance policy…” Section 2695(x) defines “third party claimant” as “any person asserting a claim against any person or the interests [sic] insured under an insurance policy.” Applying these definitions here, the facts alleged in the FAC makes clear that Lender was the only “claimant” (or the party “asserting a right under an insurance policy”) in the tender letter, not Diplomat. Lender’s “claim” was the right to a defense in the Drinkwater Action, ostensibly unrelated to Diplomat’s right to a defense in the broader Covered Lawsuits. (FAC, Exh. 12.) Accordingly, Stewart Insurance argues that its obligations under Section 2695.5(e) are limited to providing the requisite assistance to Lender, which is the party asserting the “claim.” By contrast, Diplomat’s analysis fails to clearly explain why Stewart Insurance was obligated to make disclosures under Section 2695.4(a) to Diplomat, who was neither the claimant in the tender letter nor a party to the Drinkwater Action.

 

Ultimately, the Court finds that Diplomat’s theory of breach is uncertain, unsupported by the factual and legal theories asserted in the Opposition and insufficiently tailored to Diplomat’s specific rights under the Policy. In light of the liberal policy favoring amendment of pleadings, however, the Court will permit Diplomat to amend its pleading to clarify its theory of breach. The Court notes that Stewart Insurance’s demurrer is focused primarily on the defects in Diplomat’s theory that Stewart Insurance breached its duty to defend Diplomat in the Covered Lawsuits by rejecting Lender’s tender in the Drinkwater Action. Thus, an amended pleading would benefit from narrowing and clarifying the nature and scope of the coverage that Stewart Insurance failed to provide to Diplomat (as opposed to its predecessors in interest).

 

Accordingly, Stewart Insurance’s demurrer to the second cause of action for breach of insurance contract is SUSTAINED with LEAVE TO AMEND.

 

B.            3rd Cause of Action: Breach of the Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing – SUSTINED with LEAVE TO AMEND

 

Diplomat’s breach of the implied covenant claim is also inadequately pled. To establish a breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing by an insurer, a plaintiff must allege that: (1) benefits due under the policy were withheld, and (2) the reason for withholding benefits was unreasonable or without proper cause. (Love v. Fire Ins. Exchange (1990) 221 Cal.App.3d 1136, 1151.) Where a plaintiff has “no viable breach of contract claim against [the defendant], his claim for bad faith denial of insurance benefits fails as a matter of law.” (Behnke v. State Farm General Ins. Co. (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 1443, 1470.)

 

Here, Diplomat alleges that Stewart Insurance acted in bad faith by unreasonably failing to construe the tender of claim by Lender as being from Diplomat and by breaching its duty to defend Diplomat in the Covered Lawsuits. (FAC, ¶ 66.) These allegations are essentially identical to the facts underlying Diplomat’s breach of contract claim. For the same reasons discussed above, whether Stewart Insurance’s conduct amounted to a breach of the express terms of the Policy or a breach of the implied covenant by denying benefits in bad faith, Diplomat fails to demonstrate how Stewart Insurance is liable to Diplomat in connection with the Policy. Diplomat must allege more specific factual allegations clarifying the benefits owed to Diplomat under the Policy in connection with the Covered Lawsuits and how Stewart Insurance failed to comply with its obligations under the Policy.

 

Accordingly, Stewart Insurance’s demurrer to the third cause of action for breach the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing is SUSTAINED with LEAVE TO AMEND.

 

II.       MOTION TO STRIKE – DENIED as MOOT

 

Stewart Insurance moves to strike Diplomat’s request for punitive damages from the FAC. In light of the above ruling sustaining the demurrer to both causes of action against Stewart Insurance, no remaining claim exists in the FAC to support a claim for punitive damages. Accordingly, the Court deems Stewart Insurance’s motion to strike to be MOOT.

 

III.      REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE

 

Stewart Insurance requests judicial notice of the FAC filed in this action. The Court finds the request is superfluous and DENIES the request accordingly.

 

Defendant Stewart Title Guaranty Company to serve notice of ruling. This tentative ruling (“TR”) shall be the order of the Court unless changed at the hearing and shall by this reference be incorporated into the Minute Order.
